claims.text: The high-entropy nanoalloy has an FeCoCrNiMn composition.
The initial FeCoCrNiMn nanoalloy has an FCC crystal structure.
The initial alloy has an average grain size of 10 nm.
High-temperature exposure causes a stable surface oxide layer to form on the nanoalloy.
The surface oxide layer governs the structural and chemical stability of the nanoalloy at high temperature.
The stable surface layer is a mixture of FeO, CoO, Cr2O3, NiO, and MnO.
The stable oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxidation and degradation.
Suppression of further oxidation and degradation by the oxide barrier maintains the alloy's structural and chemical stability.
At 800°C, the FeCoCrNiMn nanoalloy will exhibit a 30% lower oxidation rate than pure iron.
Pure iron has an oxidation rate of 0.5 nm/h at 800°C.
The predicted 30% reduction corresponds to an FeCoCrNiMn oxidation rate of approximately 0.35 nm/h under the stated comparison.
The prediction applies to FeCoCrNiMn nanoalloys from 700°C to 900°C for exposure times up to 20 hours.
Composition and microstructural variations may alter the predicted stability.
Degradation mechanisms other than oxidation may occur at high temperatures.
The hypothesis is falsified if the oxidation rate with a stable oxide layer is not at least 20% lower than the pure-iron baseline.

contradictions.description: The experiment specifies an inert argon atmosphere but attributes behavior to formation and continued growth of a multicomponent oxide layer without specifying an oxygen source, oxygen partial pressure, or a pre-existing oxide. This makes the proposed oxidation pathway internally underdefined.
